title: Baal
def: A Canaanite god whom the prophet Elijah rebuked his people for worshipping (37:125).
what: The Quran tells of Elijah (Ilyas) saying to his people: “Do you call upon Baal and abandon the best of creators, God, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers?” (37:125–126). Baal was the storm-god worshipped in Canaan and Phoenicia and denounced in the Hebrew Bible. Hubal was the chief idol in the Kaaba before Islam.

title: Baba Rode Shah
def: A holy man of Punjabi folklore, whose stories belong to local tradition and not to Islamic teaching.
what: Stories are told in Punjab of a seer who lived at the village of Bhoma and performed miracles for people in distress. Muslim scholars treat tales of local saints as folk tradition: they are not part of the creed, and the Quran gives its own signs to prophets alone.

title: Babel
def: The Quran mentions Babylon in the story of Harut and Marut (2:102).
what: The verse says that the devils taught people magic, and “what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut”, who warned that they were only a test (2:102). The Quran does not mention the Tower of Babel, but the Bible’s story of the confusion of languages (Genesis 11) has a different setting.

title: Babur's Will
def: A document attributed to the first Mughal emperor, urging tolerance towards Hindus; its authenticity is doubtful.
what: Babur (1483–1530) founded the Mughal empire in India. A “last will” in which he tells his son Humayun to respect Hindu sentiments and spare cows circulates in modern books, and historians doubt it. Babur’s own memoir, the Bāburnāma, is the reliable source for his views.
sources: Whether or not the will is genuine, Islamic law told Muslim rulers to respect the religions of those under their rule, and the Mughal emperor Akbar later set out a policy of broad toleration.

title: Baca
def: A name in Psalm 84:6; the Quran uses a similar name, Bakka, for Mecca (3:96).
what: “The first house established for mankind was that at Bakka, blessed and a guidance for all the worlds” (3:96). Some Muslim writers connect it with the “valley of Baca” in Psalm 84:6. Scholars, Muslim and other, differ, and nothing in Islamic belief depends on it. Muslims say Bakka is an old name of Mecca, or the site of the Kaaba within it.

title: Backbiting
def: Speaking ill of someone in his absence, which the Quran compares to eating the flesh of one’s dead brother.
what: “Do not backbite one another. Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would hate it” (49:12). The Prophet defined it: “mentioning your brother in a way he dislikes.” When asked, “and if what I say is true?”, he said, “if it is true, you have backbitten him, and if it is false you have slandered him” (Sahih Muslim).

title: Badawi, Jamal
def: A Canadian Muslim scholar and teacher, born in Egypt, known for English-language presentations of Islam.
what: Jamal Badawi (b. 1932) taught management at Saint Mary’s University in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and made a long series of television programmes on Islam in English in the 1970s and 1980s. He represents one of many modern writers explaining Islam to Western audiences.

title: Badr
def: The first major battle between the Muslims of Medina and Quraysh, in Ramadan, 2 AH (624).
what: About 313 Muslims met an army of roughly a thousand Meccans at the wells of Badr and won. The Quran recalls it: “God helped you at Badr when you were weak” (3:123), and speaks of angels aiding the believers (8:9–12). A number of Quraysh were captured.
sources: The Meccans had been fighting the Muslims since they were driven from their homes and property. The prisoners were ransomed, and a report in Ahmad says some who could not pay were released after teaching Muslim children to read.

title: Bahira
def: A Christian monk whom the young Muhammad is said to have met on a trading journey to Syria.
what: Ibn Ishaq relates that when Muhammad was about twelve and travelling with his uncle Abu Talib’s caravan, a monk named Bahira at Busra saw signs of future prophethood in him and warned his uncle to guard him. The report is in al-Tirmidhi, whose version has details that scholars question.
misread: That Bahira taught Muhammad what became the Quran.
sources: Critics have said the Quran’s teaching came from him. The Quran records a form of the accusation and answers it: “the tongue of him to whom they point is foreign, and this is clear Arabic” (16:103). The meeting was a single short stop in a caravan when Muhammad was a boy, and the Quran came to him decades later.

title: Baked bricks
def: The Quran has Pharaoh say “kindle a fire for me, Haman, upon the clay” (28:38); baked brick was in use in ancient Egypt.
what: Pharaoh tells his minister Haman to “bake clay” and build a tower to see the God of Moses (28:38). Critics say that Egyptians built in stone, not baked brick.
sources: The Bible says the Israelites in Egypt made bricks (Exodus 1:14), and fired brick has been found at Egyptian sites, so the verse is not out of place. See the Haman article for the other objection raised against this passage.

title: Balaam
def: The Biblical seer whom some commentators identify with the man described in Quran 7:175–176.
what: The Quran speaks of a man to whom God gave His signs but who “detached himself from them”, and whose likeness is “that of the dog” (7:175–176). Some early commentators say this was Bal’am, the seer of Numbers 22–24 who was hired to curse Israel. The Quran does not name him.

title: Barnabas
def: A companion of Paul in Acts; a late “Gospel of Barnabas” in which Muhammad is foretold is not an early text.
what: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus and an early Christian leader (Acts 4:36). The Gospel of Barnabas that some Muslims cite survives in Italian and Spanish manuscripts of the sixteenth century and is thought by most scholars to be a medieval work, with Islamic material in it.
sources: Many Muslim scholars and writers do not rely on it. The Muslim account of Jesus comes from the Quran and the Prophet’s sayings, and does not depend on a medieval document.

title: Barton, James L.
def: An American missionary and writer (1855–1936) who wrote on Islam and documented the Armenian massacres.
what: James L. Barton was a Congregational missionary and long-time foreign secretary of the American Board. He wrote on Muslim and Christian beliefs, and led relief work for Armenians during and after the First World War.

title: Baydawi, al-
def: A thirteenth-century Shafi’i scholar of Shiraz, author of a widely-read short commentary on the Quran.
what: Nasir al-Din al-Baydawi wrote Anwār al-tanzīl wa-asrār al-taʾwīl, a concise commentary that draws on al-Zamakhshari and others. It has been studied and annotated for centuries.

title: Bedouin
def: The nomadic Arabs; the Quran speaks of some who were hypocrites and of others who believed (9:97–99).
what: The Quran says that the Bedouins are the most severe in disbelief and hypocrisy (9:97), and then adds “and among the Bedouins are some who believe in God and the Last Day” (9:99). They are told not to say “we believe” until faith has entered their hearts (49:14).

title: Begging
def: Islam discourages begging when it can be avoided, and urges generosity to those who do beg.
what: The Prophet said “the upper hand is better than the lower hand” (Sahih al-Bukhari): the one who gives is better than the one who takes. He said that whoever asks people for money to increase his own wealth is asking for hot coals (Sahih Muslim). Begging was allowed in cases of real need. The Quran says “as for the beggar, do not repel him” (93:10).

title: Begotten
def: The Quran’s statement that God neither begets nor is begotten (112:3), directed at the belief that God has a son in a literal sense.
what: “He neither begets nor is begotten” (112:3). “It is not for God to take a son; glory be to Him” (19:35). “How could He have a son when He has no consort?” (6:101). Muslims read these as rejecting the idea of a child born to God by generation. The Bible uses “son of God” of Israel (Exodus 4:22), of kings (Psalm 2:7), and of the righteous.
sources: Muslims distinguish this from the language of the prophets, who used “son” as a metaphor of love and nearness. The Quran’s objection is to the claim that the Son shares in God’s own being, a claim it says nothing in creation can fit (19:88–93).

title: Beheading
def: The Quran’s battlefield command “strike the necks” (47:4) is about combat; the Prophet forbade mutilation, and Muslim scholars have condemned beheadings by extremists.
what: “When you meet those who disbelieve in battle, strike their necks, until you have subdued them” (47:4; also 8:12). Commentators read this as language about fighting an enemy in war. Reports in Sahih al-Bukhari say the Prophet forbade mutilating the dead and killing women and children.
sources: In 2014 more than a hundred Muslim scholars from around the world wrote an open letter to the leader of ISIS refuting its use of beheading and other practices as contrary to Islamic law. The treatment of the men of Banu Qurayza, by contrast, is reported in the biographies and discussed in its own entry.

title: Bhavishya Purana
def: A Hindu text some Muslim writers cite as foretelling Muhammad; most scholars date the passage after Islam.
what: A passage in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa speaks of a teacher from the desert whom some Muslims have identified with Muhammad. Scholars generally date the Purana in its present form to a period long after the rise of Islam, with later additions.
sources: Many Muslim scholars do not rely on it. Islam’s own evidence of the Prophet is the Quran and the record of his life, and the Quran’s claim that earlier scriptures foretold him refers to the Torah and Gospel (7:157), not to other texts.

title: Bible
def: The scripture of Christians. Muslims honour the Torah and Gospel as revealed, and hold that the Bible as it is now includes later human additions.
what: The Bible has two parts: the Old Testament (39 books in the Protestant canon) and the New Testament (27). Catholic and Orthodox churches count more books in the Old Testament. Muslims believe in the Torah given to Moses and the Gospel given to Jesus (5:44–46), and say that the Quran confirms what is true in them and guards it (5:48).
sources: The Quran tells the People of the Gospel to judge by what God revealed in it (5:47) and tells the Prophet to ask those who have read the Book before him (10:94). Muslims read the Bible with respect, and differ with Christians over the cross, the Trinity and the nature of Jesus.

title: Bid'ah
def: Innovation in religion: adding to the faith what the Prophet did not teach.
what: The Prophet said “whoever introduces into this matter of ours what is not part of it, it is rejected” (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim), and “every innovation is a going astray” (Sahih Muslim). Scholars disagree on what counts. Umar called the congregational night prayers of Ramadan “a good innovation” (Sahih al-Bukhari), and al-Shafi’i is reported to have divided innovations into praiseworthy and blameworthy.

title: Bilal
def: A former slave from Abyssinia who became the first muezzin of Islam.
what: Bilal ibn Rabah accepted Islam early and was tortured by his master Umayya ibn Khalaf, who laid a rock on his chest in the sun, until Abu Bakr bought and freed him. The Prophet appointed him to call the prayer, and he climbed on the Kaaba to call after the conquest of Mecca. His story is told as proof that the faith overrides race and rank.

title: Bin Baz, Abd al-Aziz
def: A Saudi scholar (1910–1999) who was Grand Mufti of Saudi Arabia from 1993.
what: Abd al-Aziz ibn Baz was born in Riyadh, memorised the Quran as a boy, and lost his sight in his teens. He taught and gave rulings for decades and became Grand Mufti. His fatwas are widely cited among Salafi Muslims, and other Muslims have criticised some of them, so they are an example of the range of views within the faith.

title: Biology
def: The Quran refers to living things as signs of God, including that life began in water and that plants come in pairs.
what: “We made from water every living thing” (21:30); “God created every moving creature from water” (24:45). “He made of every fruit two kinds” (13:3). Muslims see these as invitations to reflect on creation. Medieval Muslim scientists, including al-Jahiz in zoology and Ibn al-Baytar in botany, carried out detailed study of animals and plants.

title: Birth
def: The Quran describes each birth as a new creation by God (39:6).
what: “He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses” (39:6). The Quran uses childbirth as a sign of God’s power and mercy (22:5).

title: Birth rate
def: The Prophet encouraged marrying and having children, but this is not a strategy of takeover, and fertility in Muslim countries has fallen sharply.
what: A hadith in Abu Dawud tells men to marry women who are loving and fertile, “for I will boast of your numbers before the other nations”. The family and children are praised in the Quran (25:74), and contraception was allowed by most jurists (see azl).
sources: The claim that Muslims plan to take over by having children is not part of the faith. Fertility rates in Iran, Turkey, Tunisia and other Muslim-majority countries have fallen close to or below replacement level.

title: Black flag
def: Reports of black banners coming from Khorasan, used by the Abbasids and by modern extremist groups, which many scholars class as weak.
what: Hadith collections have reports of black banners that come from the east before the appearance of the Mahdi, and the Abbasid revolt of 750 used black as its colour. Hadith scholars rate the reports that mention banners from Khorasan as weak, and some as fabricated.
sources: Groups such as ISIS have used black flags, and Muslim scholars reject their claim. The flag of the Prophet’s own day is reported in different colours, and the shahada on a plain flag is a later practice.

title: Blasphemy
def: The Quran forbids mocking religion and reviling others’ gods, but sets no worldly punishment; Muslim law has differed.
what: “Do not insult those they invoke besides God, lest they insult God out of enmity and without knowledge” (6:108). Believers are told to leave a gathering where God’s signs are mocked, until they turn to another subject (4:140, 6:68). The Quran gives no earthly punishment for it.
misread: That Islam punishes all insults to the Prophet by death.
sources: Many classical jurists held that insulting the Prophet is punishable by death, and others, notably the Hanafis, distinguished and limited it. The Prophet himself left unpunished a man who said to him, “be fair, Muhammad” (Sahih al-Bukhari), and tolerated the taunts of Abdullah ibn Ubayy. Blasphemy laws in some countries today, such as Pakistan’s, are a subject of debate among Muslim scholars.

title: Borders
def: Verse 8:72 distinguishes between believers who migrated and those who did not, and puts treaty obligations first.
what: “Those who believed but did not migrate, you have no obligation of protection until they migrate; but if they ask your help in the matter of religion, you must help, except against a people with whom you have a treaty” (8:72).

title: Botros, Zakaria
def: A Coptic priest known for satellite television programmes in Arabic that are critical of Islam.
what: Zakaria Botros is an Egyptian-born Coptic priest whose Arabic-language broadcasts attack Islamic beliefs. Muslim scholars answer such criticism by argument, in the Quran’s words, “in the way that is best” (16:125).

title: Bribery
def: The Quran forbids using money to gain a ruling over another’s property (2:188), and the Prophet cursed both who gives and who takes a bribe.
what: “Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly, nor offer it to the judges so as to devour a portion of the wealth of others knowingly in sin” (2:188). The Prophet said that God curses the one who gives a bribe and the one who takes it (Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi).

title: Brotherhood
def: The Quran calls the believers brothers, and tells them to hold fast together and not to divide (3:103).
what: “The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your brothers” (49:10). “Hold fast to the rope of God all together and do not divide; and remember God’s favour to you when you were enemies and He united your hearts, so that you became brothers by His favour” (3:103). In Medina the Prophet paired each emigrant with an Ansari as brothers.

title: Bucaille, Maurice
def: A French surgeon (1920–1998) who wrote a popular book arguing that the Quran agrees with modern science.
what: Maurice Bucaille’s The Bible, the Qur’an and Science (1976) was widely read among Muslims. Critics say he reads the Quran selectively and its verses beyond what they say, and Muslim scholars are themselves divided on whether it is right to read the Quran as a source of scientific facts.

title: Bukhari, al-
def: Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari (810–870), compiler of Sahih al-Bukhari, the most respected hadith collection.
what: Born in Bukhara, he travelled widely to collect reports and is said to have spent sixteen years on his Ṣaḥīḥ. It has about 7,000 reports counting repetitions, and about 2,600 without them, chosen from a far larger number he examined. He required that narrators had met their sources, a stricter standard than some of his contemporaries.
sources: The collection is regarded by Sunni scholars as the most reliable book after the Quran. Even so, scholars have debated individual reports in it, and later critics such as al-Daraqutni pointed out a small number of them for criticism.

title: Bulleh Shah
def: A Punjabi Sufi poet (1680–1758), whose verse on divine love is sung across South Asia.
what: Abdullah Shah, known as Bulleh Shah, was born near Bahawalpur and lived at Kasur. He wrote in Punjabi in the mystical tradition, and his kāfīs are sung by Muslims, Sikhs and Hindus.

title: Byzantines
def: The Quran’s chapter “The Romans” (30) says the Byzantines, defeated by the Persians, would win “within a few years”.
what: Chapter 30 begins: “The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will be victorious within a few years” (30:2–4). The Persians captured Jerusalem in 614, and the Byzantine emperor Heraclius defeated them from 622 and finally in 627–628. Heraclius also received a letter from the Prophet, according to Sahih al-Bukhari.
sources: The Arabic word for “few” (biḍʿ) is three to nine, and Byzantine successes began within that time. Muslims treat it as an example of an unlikely statement that was borne out.

title: Badi', al-
def: A divine name meaning the Beginner of all things; also given as al-Mubdiʾ.
what: Al-Bādiʾ means the One who begins, who brings creation into being at the start. Faruqi also gives the form al-Mubdiʾ, from the same root. The name teaches that every thing was begun by God and has no origin apart from Him. The Quran speaks of God as the One who originates creation and then repeats it (85:13), and in several places it calls Him the one who begins the creation and will bring it back (10:4). The name is often thought of together with al-Muʿīd, the Restorer. Together they cover creation and resurrection, so that the beginning and the return both belong to God.
misread: That creation was set in motion and left, when the name teaches that God begins every thing and brings it back again.
sources: The Quranic phrase “He originates and repeats” (85:13) is the source commonly cited for the pair of names al-Mubdiʾ and al-Muʿīd.

title: Baghy, al-
def: A false or evil endeavour, spoiled by a false or evil intention, a false or evil result, or both.
what: Al-baghy is wrongful conduct that goes beyond its limits. Faruqi defines it as an endeavour that is false or evil because of its intention or its consequence, or both. The word can cover oppression, rebellion against rightful authority, and aggression against others. The Quran lists it with the gravest wrongs. It says that God has forbidden immoral deeds, whether open or hidden, sin, and baghy without right (7:33). Another verse says God commands justice, kindness and giving to kin, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing and baghy (16:90). The word is the reverse of ʿadl and iḥsān, which the second verse sets beside it.
misread: That the word means only political rebellion, when its range includes any wrongful transgression against right.
sources: The jurists later used bughāt, the plural form of the same root, for those who rebel against a lawful ruler, and they set rules for dealing with them.

title: Balagh, al-
def: A name of the Quran: that which has reached humankind from God.
what: Al-balāgh comes from the root meaning to arrive or to reach. As a name of the Quran, Faruqi explains, it refers to the message that has reached human beings from God. The word stresses that the Quran is a message delivered to its recipients, and the word is also tied to the task of the Messenger, which is to convey it. The Quran uses the word of itself: it says “this is a message (balāgh) for mankind” (14:52). It also describes the duty of the Messenger as plain delivery (5:99). The name therefore joins the content of revelation with the duty of conveying it, which Muslims inherit as a duty to pass the message on.
misread: That it is only a general word for “message”, when it is a name given to the Quran as the message that has reached humankind.
sources: Several verses, among them 5:67 and 5:99, describe the Prophet’s duty as balāgh, conveying what was revealed.

title: Baqi, al-
def: A divine name meaning He who exists forever and remains after all else has passed away.
what: Al-Bāqī means the Everlasting. It is a name of God and says that He alone does not end. Everything else, including every created thing, will pass away, and He will remain. Faruqi glosses it as the one who survives after all else has perished. The Quran says that everything on earth will perish, and the face of your Lord will remain, full of majesty and honour (55:26-27). Another verse says that all things perish except His face (28:88). The name reminds believers that the world is temporary and that their dependence rests on the One who is permanent.
misread: That the name means only long life, when it says that God’s existence has no end and is not like that of created things.

title: Baraka
def: To fill with the grace and approval of God.
what: Bāraka is the verb for conferring baraka, blessing. To say that God has bāraka something is to say that He has filled it with increase, goodness and His approval. People use the verb in prayer for one another, and the noun baraka names the blessing itself. The Quran uses the root of places and persons God has blessed. The opening verse of Surah al-Isra speaks of the Sacred Mosque and the farthest mosque “whose surroundings We have blessed” (17:1). The word is not tied to any object as such: blessing is God’s gift, and a believer asks for it in his dealings.
misread: That baraka is a magical property of objects, when it is a gift that comes from God alone.

title: Baraka Allah Fik
def: “May Allah bless you,” to one person (fīk) or several (fīkum), said as a compliment on any occasion.
what: The phrase means “May Allah bless you”. It is said to one person as fīk or to a group as fīkum, and Faruqi says it is a compliment suited to any occasion. A Muslim uses it to thank someone, to praise good work or to wish another well, and so it often takes the place of a plain “thank you”. The phrase turns thanks into a prayer. Instead of rewarding the other person himself, the speaker asks God, who is the source of all reward, to bless him. It uses the verb bāraka, to fill with God’s grace. A common reply is wa fīka bārak Allāh, “and may Allah bless you”.
misread: That it is only an alternative to “thank you”, when it asks God to bless the person.

title: Bari', al-
def: A divine name meaning the Creator who brings things into being.
what: Al-Bāriʾ is a name of God that means the Maker, the Creator who brings things into being. Faruqi glosses it as the Creator of all things. Muslim scholars often noted that it points to creation that is free of defect and without any previous model. The Quran names it among three: He is God, the Creator (al-Khāliq), the Maker (al-Bāriʾ) and the Fashioner (al-Muṣawwir) (59:24). In the story of Moses, his people are told to turn in repentance to their Bāriʾ (2:54). The name reminds the believer that creatures owe their existence to God and that He knows them from the beginning.
misread: That it is a duplicate of al-Khāliq, when the Quran gives it its own place beside the other names.

title: Bashir
def: A name of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him): the bearer of glad tidings.
what: Bashīr means the bearer of good news. It is one of the names of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), whom the Quran sends as a bearer of glad tidings (bashīr) and a warner (nadhīr). Good news is for those who believe and do good, while the warning concerns the result of rejecting the message. The Quran says God sent him with the truth as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner (2:119). It also says that he was sent to all humankind in this role (34:28). The title is thus tied to his mission as a messenger, and the two roles are always named together.
misread: That the Prophet’s mission was only to threaten, when the Quran gives him first the role of one who brings good news.

title: Basir, al-
def: A divine name meaning He who sees everything.
what: Al-Baṣīr means the All-Seeing. It is a name of God and it teaches that nothing is hidden from Him. Faruqi glosses it as the One who sees everything. Believers think of the name when they need to remember that their deeds are known to God in every place and at every hour, in public and in private. It teaches that no deed, however small, escapes God.

The Quran often pairs it with al-Samīʿ, the All-Hearing, as in the verse which says there is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing (42:11). The same verse protects against comparison with creatures, since God’s seeing is not like the sight of any created thing. The name is a basis for iḥsān, which a famous hadith defines as worshipping God as though one sees Him, for if one does not see Him, He sees one.
misread: That God’s sight resembles human sight, when the Quran says that nothing is like Him.
sources: The hadith of Jibril, reported by Muslim, defines iḥsān in this way.

title: Ba'th, al-
def: Resurrection, when all people are raised to face God’s judgment.
what: Al-baʿth means the raising of the dead. At the end of time God will raise all human beings from death to stand before Him for judgment. It is one of the articles of faith, together with belief in God, His angels, His books and His messengers. The Quran affirms that God will resurrect those in the graves (22:7). It answers those who deny resurrection by pointing to creation: the One who made people the first time can make them again. The resurrection is followed by reckoning and the entrance to Paradise or Hell. Belief in al-baʿth gives the believer a reason for accountability.
misread: That the afterlife is a symbol, when the Quran speaks of a real bodily raising for reckoning.

title: Batil
def: The opposite of ḥaqq: the false in belief, and the evil or wrong in conduct.
what: Bāṭil is the opposite of ḥaqq. In knowledge it is what is false, and in action it is what is evil or wrong. Faruqi pairs the two as the two ends of truth and falsehood. In law the word also describes a contract or act that has no legal force. The Quran says that the truth has come and falsehood has vanished, for falsehood is bound to vanish (17:81). It also forbids consuming wealth among yourselves bi’l-bāṭil, by unlawful means (2:188). The word thus covers false belief and wrongful dealing alike.
misread: That it only describes false statements, when it also names wrong deeds and invalid acts.
sources: In legal writing a bāṭil contract is void from the start. The Hanafi school distinguishes it from a fāsid, a defective but not void contract.

title: Batin, al-
def: A divine name meaning He who is hidden behind all phenomena; the opposite of al-Ẓāhir.
what: Al-Bāṭin means the Hidden. Faruqi explains that it names God as the One hidden behind all appearances, and gives al-Ẓāhir, the Manifest, as its opposite. The name does not say that God is absent. It says that His reality cannot be grasped by the senses, although His signs are everywhere. The Quran joins the two names with al-Awwal and al-Ākhir in a single verse: He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden (57:3). The verse ends with the statement that He has knowledge of everything. Taken together, the four names describe a God who is before and after all things and is both evident in His works and beyond sight.
misread: That God is distant, when the name says He is beyond the senses and yet close in knowledge.

title: Bay'ah
def: The nomination of the Khalifah by the leaders of the Ummah, or its endorsement by the community; also the pledge given to the Prophet (peace be upon him) at Madinah.
what: Bayʿah is a pledge of allegiance, from a root meaning to give a hand in agreement. Faruqi lists two senses. In the first it is the nomination of the khalīfa by the leaders of the ummah, or the endorsement of that choice by the community at large. In the second it is the covenant that the first Muslims of Madinah made with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), promising obedience, allegiance and protection.

The Quran says that those who pledge allegiance to the Prophet are pledging it to God (48:10), and that God was pleased with the believers who pledged under the tree (48:18). After the Prophet’s death the practice was used for the succession of the caliphs, and it remains the model for a ruler’s acceptance by the community. The oath is a mutual agreement between ruler and ruled.
misread: That it is a feudal oath of submission, when it is a mutual covenant that binds both the ruler and the community.
sources: The pledge under the tree was taken at Hudaybiyya, and Muslim writers on government have treated bayʿa as the legal basis of the caliphate.

title: Bayan, al-
def: A name of the Quran: that which is clear and makes other things clear; also eloquence of expression.
what: Al-bayān comes from a root meaning to be clear. As a name of the Quran, Faruqi says, it denotes that which is itself clear and makes other things clear. The word also names eloquence in speech and gave its name to the branch of Arabic rhetoric that studies clear and effective expression. The Quran uses the word of itself: “this is a declaration (bayān) for humankind, a guidance and an admonition for the mindful” (3:138). Another passage says that God taught humankind bayān (55:4), which here means the power of clear speech. The name expresses the claim that the Quran is both lucid and an instrument of clarity for its readers.
misread: That the Quran is obscure and needs a code to read it, when it names itself as a clear declaration.

title: Bayt, al-
def: A name of the Kaʿba, the first house built for the worship of God, raised by Ibrahim and his son Ismaʿil (peace be upon them).
what: Al-Bayt means “the House”. It is a name of the Kaʿba in Makkah, which Faruqi describes as the first house built for devotion to God, raised by Ibrahim and his son Ismaʿil (peace be upon them). Muslims face it in prayer and walk around it in the rites of ḥajj and ʿumra. The Quran says that the first house established for people was the one at Bakkah (3:96), and that Ibrahim and Ismaʿil raised its foundations (2:127). It calls the Kaʿba the Sacred House (5:97) and the Ancient House (22:29). The names stress both its sanctity and its great age, going back to the first worship of the one God.
misread: That the Kaʿba is itself worshipped, when it is the house to which Muslims turn in worship of God alone.

title: Bayyinah, al-
def: A name for each verse of the Quran, and in the plural (bayyināt) for all its verses: the clear proof that establishes truth against falsehood.
what: Al-bayyina means a clear proof. Faruqi says that the name applies to every verse of the Quran, and in the plural, bayyināt, to all its verses. Each verse is a clear evidence that establishes truth against falsehood. The word is used also for clear signs given to earlier prophets. The Quran uses bayyināt of the clear signs given to Jesus (2:87) and to other messengers. A Quranic chapter, the ninety-eighth, takes the word for its title, al-Bayyina, opening with the people who rejected faith until the clear proof came to them. The word reflects the Quran’s method of arguing from evidence.
misread: That verses are only pronouncements, when each is called a clear proof.

title: Birr, al-
def: A collective name for all conduct that God approves.
what: Al-birr is a broad word for righteousness and goodness. Faruqi defines it as the collective name for all conduct that God approves. It includes faith, worship, kindness to parents and relatives, generosity, keeping promises and patience in hardship, and it is often rendered as “piety” or “righteousness”, though neither English word fully covers its range or its stress on action.

The Quran explains it in a long verse: righteousness does not consist of turning toward east or west, but of belief in God, the last day, the angels, the Book and the prophets, giving of one’s wealth to relatives, orphans and the needy, establishing the prayer, keeping promises and being steadfast (2:177). Another verse says that people will not attain birr until they spend of what they love (3:92).
misread: That it is only outward religious show, when the Quran joins faith, worship and conduct under it.

title: Bismi Allah al-Rahman al-Rahim
def: “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful”: said at the start of any activity.
what: This phrase is called the basmala. It means “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.” Faruqi says it is said at the beginning of any activity. A Muslim starts a task, a meal, a journey or a piece of writing with it, so that the action begins under God’s name and with a reminder of His mercy. It is among the most frequently spoken phrases in Muslim life.

It opens every chapter of the Quran except the ninth, and it also appears within chapter 27, in the letter of Solomon to the queen of Sheba (27:30). The two names it ends with, al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm, both come from the root of mercy. The phrase therefore opens each undertaking by recalling God’s mercy, which is the first quality named in the Quran.
misread: That it is a ritual formula without meaning, when it places an act under God’s name and mercy.
sources: Its exact status as a verse of each chapter was discussed by scholars, and the schools differ on whether it is recited aloud in the prayer.

faruqi.term: BISMI ALLAH AL RAḤMĀN AL RAḤĪM.

title: Bismi Allah al-Rahman al-Rahim
def: “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful”: said before eating, drinking or any other activity.
what: Faruqi lists this phrase a second time, in the section on daily expressions, as a prelude to eating, drinking and other activities. It means “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.” The speaker begins his act under God’s name and acknowledges that the food, the drink and the capacity to enjoy them come from Him. The same words open the chapters of the Quran and the letter of Solomon (27:30). At meals they give the household a moment of gratitude before eating. Many Muslims teach children to say them before they begin, so that mindfulness of God is part of ordinary life from an early age.
misread: That a blessing is said only in the mosque, when this phrase attends ordinary meals and daily tasks.

faruqi.term: BISMI ALLAH AL RAḤMĀN AL RAḤĪM.

title: Bismi Allah alladhi la Ilaha illa Huwa
ar: بسم الله الذي لا إله إلا هو
tr: Bismi Allāh alladhī lā ilāha illā Huwa
def: “In the name of Allah, other than Whom there is no god”: said each time one undresses.
what: The phrase means “In the name of Allah, other than Whom there is no god.” Faruqi records that it is said each time one undresses. It places a private act under God’s name and affirms His oneness (tawḥīd) in the words lā ilāha illā Huwa, “there is no god but He”. The practice reflects the Muslim habit of beginning even small, private acts with God’s name. It is also an act of modesty, since undressing is an occasion when a person is exposed and in need of protection. The wording joins the basmala with the declaration of God’s oneness.
misread: That religious phrases belong only to public worship, when Muslims also use them in private matters.

faruqi.term: BISMI ALLAH ALLADHĪ LĀ ILAHA ILLĀ HUWA.

title: Bismi Allah Majraha wa Mursaha
def: “In the name of Allah be its course and its mooring”: said when boarding a ship, aeroplane or other vehicle.
what: The phrase means “In the name of Allah be its course and its mooring.” Faruqi gives it as the words said when boarding a ship, an aeroplane or another vehicle. Majrāhā is the moving and mursāhā the coming to rest. The traveller asks that the whole journey, from departure to arrival, be under God’s name and care. The words come from the Quranic story of Noah. He told his people to board the ark, saying that in God’s name be its course and its mooring (11:41). Muslims have taken the phrase as a general prayer for safe travel, whatever the means of transport.
misread: That it applies only to ships, when Muslims say it for any vehicle.
